newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Over 100 foreign observers for Chechen vote.
newsitem.headline: Over 100 foreign observers for Chechen vote.

text.p: More than 100 outside observers, including Russians, will monitor Monday's presidential and parliamentary elections in breakaway Chechnya, the chief European mediator in the region said on Friday.

Tim Guldimann, the Swiss diplomat in charge of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe mission in Grozny, told reporters 75 observers would work under the auspices of the OSCE. Another 40 would work independently.

The OSCE observers are from 12 of the body's member states. The independent monitors come from a range of countries, including Russia, which refuses to countenance Chechen demands for independence despite having pulled out all its troops after military reverses last year.
Guldimann also challenged charges by senior Russian officials that the Kremlin had no knowledge of OSCE funding to help the Chechen authorities pay for the organisation of voting.
Some Russian politicians say the money contravenes laws banning foreign funding of Russian election campaigns and that Guldimann should be thrown out of the country.
"We had agreed on what we were doing here with Rybkin and the Security Council," Guldimann said, referring to the Kremlin security body and its secretary, Ivan Rybkin.
Guldimann said the OSCE would spend more than $600,000 on assistance to the Chechen government to help it run the vote.

He showed reporters skin-marking devices visible only under ultra-violet light which the OSCE has provided to prevent people from voting twice. Most of the rest of the cash went on printing ballot papers and funding the observer mission.

Russian troops were sent into Moslem Chechnya in 1994 to put down its independence drive but left less than two years later after humiliating battlefield defeats. That left the region, which looks to oil refining and pipelines for its wealth, with its de facto independence in tact.
But Chechnya's separatist government is essentially bankrupt after the bloody conflict which killed tens of thousands of people and caused damage on a wide scale.
Chechen officials said on Friday they had stepped up security ahead of the vote. The observers will be accompanied by armed escorts as they tour polling stations.
